term: Insider Risk Management (Microsoft Purview)
def: A Purview solution that correlates signals such as file downloads, sharing, and printing to detect risky insider activity, including data leaks and data theft by departing users. Built-in policy templates produce risk scores and alerts for investigators.
eg: The departing-user template can use an HR connector to import resignation and termination dates. Templates also exist for risky AI usage, so it appears in AI governance scenarios.

term: Data Security Posture Management (DSPM) for AI (Microsoft Purview)
def: A Purview capability (now the classic experience, succeeded by the current Data Security Posture Management with AI observability) that gives visibility into how users and agents interact with Microsoft 365 Copilot and other generative AI apps, tracking risks such as oversharing, exfiltration, and unusual access, and recommending data protection actions drawing on DLP, labels, and insider risk.
eg: It is data-centric posture, whereas AI security posture management in Defender for Cloud is workload-centric. Match the tool to whether the scenario concerns sensitive data or AI infrastructure.

term: Finding overexposure of data in SharePoint before AI uses it
def: Overexposed SharePoint content is found with Microsoft Purview Data Security Posture Management data risk assessments (for example the weekly assessment of the top 100 sites by usage in the classic experience) and SharePoint Advanced Management data access governance reports covering permission state, sharing links and 'Everyone except external users' exposure. Findings feed remediation such as site access reviews, restricted access control and sensitivity labels.
eg: AI assistants respect existing permissions, so cleaning up oversharing is what reduces AI-driven data exposure.

term: Defender for AI services plan components
def: Threat protection for AI services is enabled per subscription (Environment settings > Defender plans > AI services, Owner or Contributor needed) and protects Microsoft Foundry workloads. Its components are suspicious prompt evidence (snippets of prompts and responses in alerts, masked if disabled), data security for AI interactions (Microsoft Purview analysis, requires a Purview license) and AI model security (scanning models in Azure Machine Learning registries for serialization vulnerabilities and malware).
eg: Turning off prompt evidence does not stop detection; it only masks the content shown in alerts.

term: Data and AI security dashboard in Defender for Cloud
def: The Data and AI security dashboard gives a subscription-level view of storage, managed databases, hosted databases and AI services, showing whether each is protected by Defender CSPM, Defender for Storage, Defender for Databases and AI threat protection, along with top alerts, recommendations, attack paths, sensitive data findings and internet-exposed data resources. Full use needs those plans, sensitive data discovery and the Security explorer role.
eg: It is the monitoring surface for AI security posture: it tells you which AI resources lack protection and where the critical risks are.

term: Foundry guardrails: risks, controls and intervention points
def: A Foundry guardrail is a named collection of controls, each defining a risk to detect, the intervention points to scan and the action to take. Intervention points are user input, tool call, tool response and output (tool call and tool response apply to agents only, and agent guardrails are in preview). Risks include hate, sexual, self-harm, violence, user prompt attacks, indirect attacks, protected material and PII. A guardrail can apply to many models and agents, and creating one needs the Foundry Account Owner role.
eg: Tool call and tool response intervention points are what stop an injected instruction from making an agent call a tool it should not.

term: Configuring AI Gateway for Microsoft Foundry
def: In the Foundry portal, Manage > AI Gateway > Add AI Gateway attaches Azure API Management to a Foundry resource to apply token limits, quotas and governance to model deployments. Create new makes a Basic v2 instance for development and testing; an existing instance must be a v2 tier in the same Entra tenant and subscription. New projects get the gateway enabled by default and existing projects are added manually. For a Foundry resource with public access disabled, the APIM instance must also be private.
eg: Foundry role names changed: Azure AI User, Owner, Account Owner and Project Manager are now Foundry User, Owner, Account Owner and Project Manager, with the same permissions.

term: Managing agents in the Microsoft 365 admin center (security view)
def: Security teams govern Microsoft 365 agents from Agents > All agents in the admin center: the registry shows ownerless and unmanaged agents, requests are reviewed before publishing, and an agent can be blocked, deleted (30-day recovery) or reassigned. AI Administrator can manage agents and Copilot settings, while Security Administrator and Security Reader see the registry and insights without changing agents.
eg: Block stops use immediately; the stronger lifecycle control is requiring approval so unreviewed agents never become available.

term: Managing Entra Agent ID access with access packages and sponsors
def: Agent access is granted through entitlement management access packages that bundle group memberships, directory roles and API permissions with approval and expiry, and every agent identity needs at least one business sponsor. Owners administer the agent technically. Lifecycle Workflows can transfer sponsorship to a manager when a sponsor leaves. Extending Entra protections to agents requires Agent 365 licensing.
eg: Agents should not hold standing permissions granted ad hoc; the access package makes the grant time-bound and reviewable.

term: Real-time protection for Copilot Studio agents with Defender
def: Defender for AI agents, onboarded with Agent 365, enables discovery, posture assessment and threat detection. For Copilot Studio, real-time protection is switched on in the Defender portal (Settings > Security for AI > Get started) and finished by a Power Platform administrator; it scans agent tool invocations at runtime, blocks suspicious behavior or cross-prompt injection and raises an alert. The Microsoft 365 connector is needed for alerts and hunting in the portal.
eg: Runtime blocking works even without the connector, but without it the incident trail does not reach the Defender portal.

term: Trusted launch: Secure Boot, vTPM and integrity monitoring
def: Trusted launch strengthens generation 2 Azure VMs with Secure Boot (verified boot loaders, kernels and drivers), a virtual TPM that holds measurements and keys, and boot integrity monitoring through attestation. It defends against bootkits and rootkits and is the default for newly created generation 2 VMs and scale sets. The VM's security type setting is Standard, Trusted launch or Confidential.
eg: Existing generation 2 VMs can have it enabled afterward, and generation 1 VMs can be upgraded to generation 2 with Trusted launch.

term: Azure Machine Configuration
def: Machine Configuration, a feature of Azure Policy, audits or configures operating system settings as code on Azure VMs and Azure Arc-enabled machines. Assignment modes are Audit, Apply and Monitor, and Apply and Autocorrect, which brings a drifted machine back into conformance. Results appear on the Guest assignments page and in Azure Policy compliance.
eg: It enforces what is inside the guest operating system (for example a TLS setting), which ordinary Azure Policy on the resource properties cannot reach.

term: Agentless scanning for VMs in Defender for Servers
def: Agentless scanning analyzes snapshots of VM disks without installing anything, covering vulnerability assessment, malware scanning, secrets scanning and posture checks. It is part of Defender for Servers Plan 2 (and Defender CSPM), while Plan 1 focuses on the endpoint detection and response integration with Defender for Endpoint.
eg: Agentless coverage is useful for machines where an agent cannot be installed, but runtime EDR protection still needs the Defender for Endpoint sensor.

term: Defender Vulnerability Management for Azure VMs
def: Defender for Servers includes Microsoft Defender Vulnerability Management as the vulnerability assessment solution, assessing installed software and OS vulnerabilities on Azure VMs, Arc-enabled servers and multicloud machines, with the premium capabilities in Plan 2. Findings surface as recommendations and in the cloud security graph, and the assessment source can be changed under the plan's settings.
eg: Choose the integrated Defender Vulnerability Management solution unless there is a specific need for a third-party scanner.

term: Azure Container Registry security controls
def: Hardening Azure Container Registry means disabling the admin user and anonymous pull, authenticating with Microsoft Entra identities and the AcrPull and AcrPush roles, using the Premium SKU for private endpoints, network rules and customer-managed keys, and scanning images with Defender for Containers. Repository-scoped permissions can limit tokens to specific repositories.
eg: Private link and customer-managed keys are Premium features, so a requirement for either changes the SKU choice.

term: Securing Azure Container Instances and Azure Container Apps
def: Container Instances can be deployed into a virtual network subnet without a public IP, use managed identities to reach Key Vault and registries, and keep sensitive values in secure environment variables or secret volumes. Container Apps use an internal environment with VNet integration for private ingress, built-in authentication with Microsoft Entra, IP restrictions on ingress, managed identity and Key Vault secret references.
eg: In both services, prefer managed identity over credentials stored in the container definition.

term: Azure Functions security: authentication and network access
def: For Functions, HTTP trigger authorization levels (anonymous, function or admin keys) are only a coarse gate; App Service authentication with Microsoft Entra ID provides real user or app authentication. Network access is restricted with access restrictions or private endpoints for inbound traffic and VNet integration for outbound traffic, and managed identity plus Key Vault references avoid secrets in app settings. HTTPS-only and the latest TLS should be enforced.
eg: A function key is a shared secret, not an identity: use Entra authentication when you need to know who is calling.

term: Azure Logic Apps security
def: Logic Apps request triggers can be limited by allowed caller IP ranges and by OAuth with Microsoft Entra authorization policies instead of relying only on the SAS in the callback URL. Managed identity authenticates connectors without stored credentials, secure inputs and outputs hide sensitive values from run history, and Standard logic apps support private endpoints and VNet integration.
eg: Anyone holding the full callback URL with its SAS can invoke a request trigger, so treat it as a secret.

term: API Management policies for back-end API protection
def: API Management protects back ends with inbound policies such as validate-jwt (token validation), ip-filter, rate-limit and quota, along with subscription keys and client certificate validation, and backend authentication with managed identity or certificates. Deploying the instance in a virtual network and restricting the back end to accept traffic only from API Management stops callers bypassing the gateway.
eg: Subscription keys identify consumers but do not authenticate users; validate-jwt is what enforces Entra authentication.

term: Azure Bastion SKUs
def: Bastion has Developer, Basic, Standard and Premium SKUs. Developer is a free option for connecting to a single VM without a dedicated subnet, Basic and Standard are dedicated deployments in the AzureBastionSubnet (Standard adds features such as native client support, IP-based connection and scaling), and Premium adds capabilities such as session recording and private-only deployment.
eg: Pick the SKU from the required feature: session recording or private-only access means Premium.

term: Microsoft Defender for Cloud Secure Score
def: A percentage score that aggregates how many recommended security controls an environment has actually implemented, weighted by each recommendation's potential impact. Improving secure score means resolving the underlying recommendations, not the score itself.
eg: Secure Score is a prioritization tool, not a compliance certification — a high score reflects following Microsoft's general best-practice recommendations, which is different from passing a specific named regulatory standard.

term: Microsoft Defender for Cloud plans
def: Defender for Cloud's free tier covers basic posture management (recommendations, secure score). Enabling specific paid Defender plans per resource type (Servers, Storage, SQL, Containers, Key Vault, App Service, Resource Manager) adds workload-specific threat detection and advanced capabilities for that resource type.
eg: Plans are enabled independently per resource type at the subscription level — enabling Defender for Storage does not also enable Defender for SQL, so a scenario needing threat detection on both requires enabling both plans explicitly. DNS threat detection is no longer a separate standalone plan for new subscriptions — it now comes bundled into Defender for Servers Plan 2.

term: Just-in-time (JIT) VM access
def: A Defender for Cloud feature that locks down a VM's management ports (like RDP/SSH) by default, only opening them for a specific requester, source IP, and time window when access is explicitly requested and approved.
eg: JIT reduces the attack surface of exposed management ports without requiring Bastion — but Bastion removes the need for a public IP entirely, while JIT still allows temporary direct access to a port that could carry a public IP if one exists.

term: Adaptive application controls
def: A Defender for Cloud feature that uses machine learning to build an allowlist of known-safe applications for a group of VMs, then alerts (or can enforce) when an application outside that allowlist attempts to run. Microsoft has deprecated the Log Analytics agent-based version of this feature, so treat it as a legacy capability that older material and exam items may still reference.
eg: This is application allowlisting delivered as a managed, ML-driven recommendation rather than something manually enumerated application-by-application, which is what distinguishes it from a hand-configured allowlist policy.

term: Regulatory compliance dashboard
def: A Defender for Cloud feature that maps your environment against specific regulatory or industry standards (like PCI DSS, ISO 27001, NIST), showing which controls pass, fail, or are not applicable, and lets you add custom standards.
eg: This is distinct from Secure Score: Secure Score reflects general best practice, while the compliance dashboard reflects standing against a specific named standard an organization may be contractually or legally required to meet.

term: Microsoft Sentinel data connectors
def: Data connectors ingest log and event data from sources — Azure services, Microsoft 365, on-premises systems, and third-party/multicloud platforms — into the Log Analytics workspace that backs a Sentinel instance, where it becomes queryable and can drive analytics rules.
eg: Sentinel has no data to analyze without connectors ingesting logs first — connecting a source is always the prerequisite step before writing an analytics rule or hunting query against that data.

term: Sentinel analytics rules: scheduled vs. near-real-time vs. Fusion
def: Scheduled analytics rules run a KQL query on a set interval and generate an incident on matches. Near-real-time (NRT) rules run continuously for faster detection on a narrower set of supported queries. Fusion uses machine learning to correlate multiple low-fidelity signals across different sources into a single, higher-confidence incident.
eg: Fusion's value is correlating otherwise-unremarkable individual alerts (e.g., an odd sign-in plus an unusual resource deployment) into one incident reflecting a likely multi-stage attack, which a single scheduled rule looking at one data source alone would not catch.

term: Sentinel incidents vs. workbooks vs. hunting queries
def: An incident is a case created from one or more triggered alerts, grouping related evidence for investigation. A workbook is an interactive visualization/report built from the underlying data. A hunting query is a proactive, manually run KQL search for threats that have not yet triggered any analytics rule or incident.
eg: Hunting is explicitly proactive — you run a hunting query looking for evidence of compromise before any confirmed incident exists, as opposed to investigating an incident that already exists because a rule fired.

term: Sentinel playbooks (SOAR)
def: A playbook is a Logic App that orchestrates an automated response, like disabling a user account, isolating a VM, or posting a notification to a Teams channel. It runs automatically when an automation rule invokes it (on incident creation or update, or on alert creation), or an analyst can run it manually; attaching playbooks directly inside an analytics rule (the classic method) has been retired in favor of automation rules.
eg: Playbooks are what turn Sentinel from a detection tool into a SOAR (Security Orchestration, Automation, and Response) platform — detection without a playbook still requires a human to take the remediation action manually.

term: Log Analytics workspace and KQL
def: A Log Analytics workspace is the storage and query backend that both Azure Monitor and Microsoft Sentinel are built on. Kusto Query Language (KQL) is the query language used to search, filter, and analyze the log data stored there.
eg: Sentinel does not have its own separate log store — it is deployed onto (and queries) a Log Analytics workspace, which is why enabling Sentinel on a workspace that already collects other Azure Monitor logs makes that data available to Sentinel too.

term: Azure Monitor alerts and action groups
def: An Azure Monitor alert rule evaluates a signal (metric, log query, or activity log event) against a condition and fires when met. An action group defines what happens when an alert fires — email, SMS, webhook, Azure Function, Logic App, and more — decoupled from the alert rule so the same action group can be reused across many rules.
eg: Separating the alert condition from the action group means updating who gets notified (e.g., a new on-call engineer) only requires editing the action group once, not every alert rule that references it.

term: Connecting hybrid and multicloud resources to Defender for Cloud
def: Defender for Cloud can extend coverage beyond Azure using Azure Arc (for on-premises/other-cloud servers) and native multicloud connectors for AWS and GCP, bringing their workloads under the same recommendations, secure score, and Defender plans.
eg: The native AWS/GCP connectors give agentless posture coverage (recommendations and secure score) for cloud resources without Arc, but server-level protection such as Defender for Servers needs the machine to be Arc-enabled — and an on-premises server is normally brought in through Arc as well.

term: Zero Trust principles
def: Verify explicitly, use least-privilege access, and assume breach — treating every request as coming from an untrusted network regardless of where it originates, rather than trusting anything just because it’s "inside the perimeter."
eg: Continuous Access Evaluation (CAE) and just-in-time (JIT) VM access are both concrete implementations of "assume breach" and "least privilege" in practice, not abstract ideas on their own.

term: Workbooks in Microsoft Sentinel
def: Interactive, customizable reports built from KQL queries against Sentinel data connectors, used for ongoing operational visibility (like tracking a specific threat category over time) rather than one-off investigation.
eg: A workbook is a dashboard you keep coming back to; an analytics rule (scheduled, near-real-time, or Fusion) is instead an ongoing detection that fires an alert whenever its condition is met.

term: Sentinel automation rules
def: Automation rules run centrally across one or more analytics rules before any playbook fires, letting an analyst auto-assign, tag, suppress, or close incidents based on simple conditions, then optionally hand off to one or more playbooks (Logic Apps) for the actual remediation actions. They are also the supported way to run a playbook automatically, now that attaching playbooks directly to an analytics rule has been retired.
eg: Ordering matters: automation rules execute in a defined sequence, and each rule sees the incident as the earlier rules left it — so once a rule has closed an incident, a later rule whose conditions need an open or New incident no longer matches it.

term: Microsoft Defender for Cloud DevOps security
def: Defender for Cloud's DevOps security connects source-control platforms (GitHub, Azure DevOps, GitLab) to scan for exposed secrets, misconfigured pipelines, and vulnerable dependencies before code ever reaches a running Azure resource.
eg: This extends Zero Trust principles upstream of runtime: instead of only assuming breach and verifying explicitly once a workload is already live, it catches a hardcoded credential or an insecure pipeline setting at the source before it can ever be exploited.

term: Microsoft Defender for Cloud attack path analysis
def: Attack path analysis uses the cloud security graph to identify exploitable chains — like an internet-facing VM with a vulnerability that has a role assignment reaching a storage account holding sensitive data — and ranks them by real exploitability, not just individual finding severity.
eg: This is what separates it from the regulatory compliance dashboard: that dashboard checks configuration against a named standard in isolation, while attack path analysis specifically models whether findings chain together into an actual reachable path to something valuable.

term: Defender for Cloud governance rules
def: Assigns an owner and a remediation SLA (due date) to a security recommendation, and can escalate or surface a report when that assignment goes overdue — driving accountability for who actually fixes a finding, rather than leaving every recommendation sitting unowned in a shared list.
eg: A governance rule does not remediate anything by itself — it only assigns ownership and a deadline; an owner, or separate automation, still has to actually perform the fix.

term: Microsoft Sentinel UEBA (User and Entity Behavior Analytics)
def: Builds a behavioral baseline for each user and entity, like typical sign-in times, locations, and resources accessed, and flags deviations from that individual baseline — complementing scheduled, near-real-time, and Fusion analytics rules, which look for known patterns or cross-source correlation rather than a deviation from one entity's own normal behavior.
eg: UEBA can flag an insider-style anomaly, like a user suddenly accessing resources they have legitimate permission to but never normally touch, that a scheduled rule looking for a known attack signature would never be written to catch.

term: Microsoft Sentinel watchlists
def: Reusable named lists of data, such as known-bad IP addresses, terminated employee names, or a set of high-value asset identifiers, imported once and referenced across analytics rules, hunting queries, and workbooks, instead of hard-coding the same values separately into every query that needs them.
eg: Updating a watchlist's values once, like removing an employee after they're reinstated, automatically changes every analytics rule and hunting query that references it, rather than requiring someone to track down and edit each query individually.

term: Secure Score vs. compliance dashboard vs. Compliance Manager
def: Secure Score reflects Defender for Cloud's general infrastructure best-practice posture. The regulatory compliance dashboard maps that same infrastructure posture against one specific named standard, like ISO 27001. Microsoft Purview Compliance Manager's compliance score is a separate, broader assessment spanning data governance, organizational, and documented policy controls across Microsoft 365 and Azure — not just infrastructure configuration.
eg: These three similarly-named percentages are easy to mix up on purpose: knowing which tool produced a given score, and what scope that score actually covers, matters more than recognizing that each one is simply 'a compliance-sounding number.'

term: Microsoft Sentinel data retention: interactive vs. long-term (archive) retention
def: Interactive retention keeps ingested log data immediately queryable by analytics rules, hunting queries, and workbooks for a configured period. Long-term (archive) retention keeps that same data stored at lower cost beyond that period (Microsoft's current guidance describes this as the analytics tier, with 90 days of interactive retention by default, plus the Sentinel data lake tier for long-term data), but it is not directly queryable without first running a search job or restoring it back to interactive retention.
eg: A team planning for years of compliance retention alongside ongoing detection needs to plan for that restore step explicitly — archived data is not instantly queryable the way interactive data is, even though it still technically exists in the workspace.

term: Azure Policy effects (Audit, Deny, Modify, DeployIfNotExists)
def: Azure Policy evaluates resources against rules at a scope, and the effect decides what happens on non-compliance. Audit records a compliance entry, Deny blocks the create or update, Modify changes properties such as tags, and DeployIfNotExists deploys a related resource, such as a diagnostic setting, when it is missing.
prompt: Azure Policy evaluates resources against rules at a scope, and the effect decides what happens on non-compliance. Audit records a compliance entry, Deny blocks the create or update, Modify changes properties such as tags, and _____ deploys a related resource, such as a diagnostic setting, when it is missing.
eg: Only Deny stops a bad resource from being created. Audit merely reports, and fixing resources that already exist with Modify or DeployIfNotExists requires a remediation task.

term: Azure Policy initiative (policy set)
def: An initiative is a group of related policy definitions assigned together as one unit, with shared parameters, so a goal such as a regulatory standard is applied and tracked as a single assignment instead of dozens of separate ones.
eg: Defender for Cloud standards such as the Microsoft cloud security benchmark are delivered as initiatives. Assign one at a management group so every child subscription inherits it.

term: Azure Policy remediation task
def: Azure Policy does not fix existing non-compliant resources by itself. A remediation task applies the DeployIfNotExists template or Modify operation to them, using a managed identity that must hold the Azure RBAC roles the policy requires.
eg: A remediation that fails usually means the policy's managed identity lacks the needed role. New resources are handled when they are created, but existing ones wait for a task.

term: Defender CSPM vs. Foundational CSPM
def: Foundational CSPM is free in Defender for Cloud and provides asset discovery, security recommendations, secure score, and assessment against the Microsoft cloud security benchmark. The paid Defender CSPM plan adds attack path analysis, cloud security explorer for querying the cloud security graph, agentless machine scanning, and governance.
eg: Recommendations and secure score need no paid plan, but attack path analysis and cloud security explorer do. A scenario asking for attack paths means Defender CSPM must be enabled.

term: Defender for Servers Plan 1 vs. Plan 2
def: Plan 1 provides endpoint detection and response on servers through Microsoft Defender for Endpoint integration. Plan 2 includes everything in Plan 1 and adds further capabilities, including just-in-time VM access and file integrity monitoring.
eg: If a scenario needs just-in-time VM access or file integrity monitoring, Plan 2 is required. If it only needs endpoint detection and response on servers, Plan 1 is enough.

term: Microsoft cloud security benchmark (MCSB)
def: MCSB is Microsoft's set of cloud-agnostic security controls and best practices, the successor to the Azure Security Benchmark renamed in October 2022. It includes implementation guidance for Azure, AWS, and GCP and maps to frameworks such as CIS, NIST SP 800-53, and PCI DSS.
prompt: _____ is Microsoft's set of cloud-agnostic security controls and best practices, the successor to the Azure Security Benchmark renamed in October 2022. It includes implementation guidance for Azure, AWS, and GCP and maps to frameworks such as CIS, NIST SP 800-53, and PCI DSS.
eg: It is the standard Defender for Cloud assesses by default once a subscription is onboarded, and it drives the recommendations behind secure score.

term: Log Analytics access modes: workspace-context vs. resource-context
def: In workspace-context mode a user queries the workspace and sees all tables they have permission to. In resource-context mode a user queries through a resource, resource group, or subscription and sees only logs for resources they can access, using granular Azure RBAC. The workspace access control mode must allow resource permissions.
eg: To let an application team read only their own VM logs in a shared central workspace, use resource-context access instead of granting them rights on the whole workspace.

term: Azure Monitor diagnostic settings and the Activity log
def: A diagnostic setting routes resource logs and platform metrics to a Log Analytics workspace, a storage account, an event hub, or a partner solution. Resource logs are not collected until a setting exists, while the Activity log of subscription-level events is collected automatically.
eg: To get Azure Firewall or Key Vault logs into Sentinel, create a diagnostic setting that targets the workspace. A storage account suits cheap long-term retention, and an event hub feeds an external SIEM.

term: Microsoft Sentinel threat intelligence (STIX and TAXII)
def: Sentinel can import threat indicators, such as malicious IP addresses, domains, and file hashes, and match them against ingested logs. STIX is the standard format for describing threat data, and TAXII is the protocol for sharing it; the TAXII data connector pulls indicators from TAXII 2.0 or 2.1 servers.
eg: Connecting an industry sharing group's TAXII feed turns its published indicators into detections against your own logs. The Threat Intelligence solution in the Content hub provides the connectors.

term: Microsoft Defender XDR
def: Defender XDR is a unified pre- and post-breach defense suite that correlates signals from Defender for Endpoint, Defender for Office 365, Defender for Identity, Defender for Cloud Apps, and Microsoft Entra ID Protection into single incidents, with automated investigation and response.
eg: It specializes in Microsoft endpoint, identity, email, and app signals, while Sentinel is the broader SIEM that can ingest those incidents plus logs from everywhere else.

term: Security Copilot capacity: provisioned and overage SCUs
def: Security Copilot runs on Security Compute Units. Customers outside Microsoft 365 E5 and E7 provision capacity (minimum one SCU, billed hourly, refreshed each full clock hour, unused units expire) and can add overage capacity, consumed as used up to a maximum or unlimited. Microsoft 365 E5 and E7 customers are auto-provisioned with a default capacity. Capacity provisioning needs an Azure Contributor or Owner role and at least Security Administrator in the tenant.
eg: When provisioned SCUs run out, requests stop unless overage capacity is configured.

term: Security Copilot roles and permissions
def: Security Copilot has two platform roles, owner and contributor, which are not Microsoft Entra roles and grant access only to platform features, never to security data. At least two owners are always kept, and Global Administrator, Security Administrator, Billing Administrator and some Intune and Purview roles inherit owner access. Plugins use on-behalf-of authentication, so what a user can retrieve is limited by their own Entra and Azure RBAC permissions.
eg: Assigning someone the contributor role does not let them read Sentinel data; they also need the Sentinel role.

term: Security Copilot plugins
def: Plugins extend Security Copilot with data and actions from Microsoft and non-Microsoft products. Owners decide whether contributors can add custom plugins for themselves (user scope) or for everyone in the workspace (tenant scope), and can restrict preinstalled plugin availability. A plugin only returns data that the signed-in user is permitted to see in the underlying product.
eg: Making a custom plugin available to the organization is an owner-controlled decision, because it extends what Security Copilot can reach.

term: Security Copilot agents and Security Store
def: Security Copilot agents are autonomous or triggered workflows that run for a security task. Microsoft builds agents into Defender, Entra, Intune and Purview, partners publish agents, and the Security Store is where agents are discovered. To set up an agent the user chooses an identity, preferably a dedicated agent identity, supplies parameters and the agent's required plugins are enabled. Agents consume SCUs when they run.
eg: An agent identity limits the agent to what it needs, whereas reusing a person's account means the agent inherits all of that person's access.

term: Creating Microsoft Sentinel workspaces and the Defender portal move
def: Microsoft Sentinel is enabled on a Log Analytics workspace, and one workspace or several can be used depending on region, retention and access separation needs. Sentinel is generally available in the Microsoft Defender portal, including without Defender XDR, and after March 31, 2027 it will no longer be supported in the Azure portal. Workspaces connected to Defender manage tiering and retention in the Defender portal.
eg: New designs should plan for the Defender portal experience, since the Azure portal experience has a retirement date.

term: Microsoft Sentinel roles
def: Sentinel uses Azure RBAC: Reader views data and incidents, Responder also manages incidents, Contributor also creates and edits content and manages the content hub, Playbook Operator runs playbooks, and Automation Contributor is a service role that lets Sentinel add playbooks to automation rules. Authoring playbooks needs Logic App Contributor. Assign roles at the resource group containing the workspace for the best coverage; the Sentinel data lake uses Microsoft Entra roles.
eg: Never assign Automation Contributor to people: it exists so Sentinel itself can run playbooks from automation rules.

term: Content hub solutions in Microsoft Sentinel
def: The content hub is the place to discover and install solutions, which bundle data connectors with related analytics rules, workbooks, hunting queries and playbooks, as well as standalone content. Installing a solution gives the connector and content in one step, and solutions can be updated or deleted later. Installing and managing content needs the Sentinel Contributor role.
eg: Install the product's solution first, then configure the connector it provides.

term: Microsoft data connectors for Azure resources
def: Connectors for Azure and Microsoft sources, such as Microsoft Entra ID, Azure Activity, Microsoft Defender for Cloud and Azure Key Vault, bring logs into Sentinel by turning on diagnostic settings or service-to-service connections, often applied at scale through Azure Policy. Connecting needs write permission on the workspace plus the source's own permissions.
eg: A connector that appears connected but shows no data usually points to a missing diagnostic setting or role on the source side.

term: Syslog and Common Event Format collection with Azure Monitor Agent
def: Linux devices and appliances that cannot run an agent send Syslog or CEF messages to a Linux forwarder VM running Azure Monitor Agent, which uses a data collection rule to forward them to the workspace. Sentinel provides the Syslog via AMA and Common Event Format via AMA connectors, usually installed through the relevant solution in the content hub. Outbound port 443 must be open from the agent.
eg: The appliance sends to the forwarder on port 514; the forwarder, not the appliance, talks to the workspace.

term: Windows Security events via AMA and data collection rules
def: The Windows Security Events via AMA connector uses data collection rules to choose which events to collect, with presets or custom XPath filters that cut ingestion cost at the source. Machines outside Azure need Azure Arc first. Events land in the SecurityEvent table, which built-in Windows analytics rules query.
eg: Filtering in the DCR saves money, but dropping an event ID that an analytics rule needs silently disables that detection.

term: Windows Event Forwarding (WEF) and Windows Forwarded Events
def: For Windows Event Forwarding, source machines send events to a Windows Event Collector (WEC) server that runs Azure Monitor Agent, and the Windows Forwarded Events connector ingests them. These events are written to the WindowsEvent table, not SecurityEvent, so built-in rules that query SecurityEvent will not match unless they are adapted or the Windows Security Events connector is used.
eg: WEF reduces the number of agents to manage, at the cost of table differences for detection content.

term: Custom log tables and data collection rule transformations
def: A custom table (name ending in _CL) stores data that no built-in table fits. Data arrives through a data collection rule, either from an agent collecting text logs or from the Logs Ingestion API called with an app registration that has rights on the DCR. The DCR can include a transformation that reshapes or filters records before they reach the table, and creating the table in the portal creates the DCR for you.
eg: Transformations are the cost-control point for custom data: remove noisy columns or rows before ingestion.

term: Permissions for automation rules and playbooks
def: An automation rule can run a playbook only if Sentinel has permission to the Logic App, granted by giving the Microsoft Sentinel Automation Contributor role on the playbook's resource group. The playbook's own connections should use a managed identity with only the roles it needs, such as Sentinel Responder to update incidents. Users who run playbooks manually need Playbook Operator.
eg: A rule that silently fails to trigger a playbook is most often a missing Automation Contributor assignment.

term: Microsoft Sentinel retention: analytics tier and data lake tier
def: Sentinel has an analytics tier for primary security data, with interactive retention of 90 days by default and up to two years, supporting analytics rules and unlimited queries, and a data lake tier for high-volume secondary data kept cost-effectively for long periods, queried with KQL and summarized into the analytics tier with KQL jobs. Data kept longer in total than the analytics period remains available in the data lake tier.
eg: Choose by use: detections and frequent hunting need the analytics tier, while verbose firewall or storage logs belong in the data lake.

term: Querying Microsoft Purview Audit in Defender XDR
def: Defender XDR and Defender for Endpoint activities, such as isolating a device, creating an indicator, changing security roles or editing a custom detection, are recorded in the audit log, which Microsoft Defender reads from the Microsoft Purview auditing solution. Auditing must be turned on in Purview, and searching needs the Audit Logs or View-Only Audit Logs role. Search jobs keep running after the browser closes.
eg: Audit answers who changed what in the security tooling itself, which is different from hunting for attacker activity.

term: Defender External Attack Surface Management in Defender CSPM
def: Defender for Cloud integrates Defender External Attack Surface Management at no extra license inside the Defender CSPM plan, running outside-in scans that discover internet-facing cloud resources, feeding attack paths that start from internet-exposed IP addresses and cloud security explorer queries. Standalone EASM adds discovery of assets across the wider public attack surface.
eg: Inside-out CSPM tells you what is misconfigured; EASM adds what an attacker can see from outside.
